We see your sales wins, announcements, discussions, and questions.
And one theme always sparks the most debate: pricing.
How was the price decided? Wasn’t it too low? Too high?

Pricing a domain is neither pure science nor pure guesswork. Most of the time, it’s a mix of data, strategy, timing… and yes, sometimes just a gut feeling 😉

So we thought we’d share some of the key steps usually taken when setting prices:
1️⃣ Benchmarking against comparable sales
First stop for many sellers: looking at what similar names have sold for. Same length, same kind of keyword, same TLD. Public sales databases help set a realistic range and keep expectations right.

2️⃣ Checking appraisal tools 
Algorithms, search volume, past sales… these tools crunch the data and spit out a number. Helpful as a ballpark range, but better treat them as just one signal, not the final word.

3️⃣Deciding on a “no lower than this” price
Defining the lowest figure to accept upfront stops panic-selling and gives confidence in negotiations.

4️⃣ Defining the strategy
A fixed Buy It Now price can make sales quicker and easier, while leaving a domain open to offers gives flexibility and sometimes a higher final price. Many domainers combine both.
And there’s also Lease To Own, which opens doors for more buyers while keeping the total sale value high.

5️⃣Accounting the fees
Holding a domain for years adds up in renewals. On top of that, marketplace commissions can reshape pricing.
For example, if a domain sells for $10,000, a 20–30% fee leaves the seller with only $7,000–$8,000. By contrast, a 5% fee (like with SellerHub) means $9,500 in pocket.

6️⃣ Considering extensions 
.com remains the gold standard, valued for trust and universal recognition. But niche TLDs like .ai, .io, or .co have grown popular with startups and can command significant prices. Following trends and demand is essential.

7️⃣ Revisiting the pricing
Market conditions shift, new industries rise, and keyword demand changes. Many sellers revisit their pricing regularly – what looks premium today might look regular tomorrow if demand surges.

Pricing domains has no single formula – and that’s what makes domaining exciting, right?
But what’s in common is balancing data with strategy, adjusting as the market evolves, and constant learning.

Every sale, big or small, is part of the bigger journey. Once it’s sold, it’s no longer about what could have been, but about where you’ll go next.
Curious to know – what other factors do you usually weigh when deciding on prices? 👇

With Spaceship’s SellerHub growing every day, we thought we’d examine the history of domaining. What lessons can we learn from four decades of buying and selling domains?

1985: The very first .com, symbolics .com, was registered. The DNS system made the previous numbers-based system more memorable. At the time, registering a domain was free, and no one could know its potential.

Early to mid-1990s: Start of the .com boom. Interest in registering domains spiked as more people saw their potential. Generic words, like “loans” or “travel” were seen as particularly valuable. Quickly, domains became Internet real estate. whisky .com was one of the domains claimed for free. It would sell in 2014 for $3.1 million.

1995: Domains were monetized for the first time. It was now around $50 a year for a domain. This change cemented their potential as a commodity – a definitive sign for business-savvy folks that there was money to be made.

Late 1990s: The .com boom was in full swing. Around 1997, more established secondary marketplaces began to appear, replacing what had previously been a more informal reselling market where domains were bought and sold by email.

1999: A seminal moment for domaining, as business .com sold for $7.5 million. The Los Angeles Times noted that “selling names for $1 million is going to be an everyday event…”

Early 2000s: Domaining became mainstream. No longer a hobbyist pastime, it was a full-blown industry. Domain parking became common practice – a way of monetizing naturally high-traffic domains using ads.

2005: Marchex bought the entire portfolio of domainer Yun Ye for a jaw-dropping $164 million. At one time, the portfolio was reported to generate $280 million in ad revenue. Eventually, changes in search engine operation cut this kind of ad revenue potential, leading domainers like Marchex to exit the market. They resold their portfolio in 2015 for just $28 million. The lesson was clear: The domain market must adapt like any other.

Early 2010s: The introduction of General TLDs created a whole new market, with some selling for significant sums. Over a thousand new domains (including .app, .tech, .io) came to prominence. While this flooded the market with more “virtual plots”, prices remained buoyant, showing demand drives value, not just supply.

Mid 2010s: Around 2015-16, there was an increase in “brandable” domain marketplaces, catering to a wave of startups seeking short, catchy names (rather than English words), like Instagram and Etsy. It was a different game from hunting the million-dollar generics, but a viable new money-making strategy.

2015: Chinese investors entered the market in a big way. They traded domains like stocks, causing prices to surge. They particularly valued short “CHIP” domains (ones that didn’t include vowels or the letter V). Prices for 4-letter .coms, previously costing $100 or less, shot up to thousands of dollars. Sales of number-based .coms also surged.

The 2020s and beyond: Domaining continues to evolve today. There are undoubtedly more changes on the horizon. But what lessons can we take from four decades of domaining?

🔹 Decide on your method: History is bursting with examples of successful domainers with very different approaches. Some sell a few domains for seven-figure figures, while others get smaller (but more regular) profits from turning over thousands of lower-value domains. Pick the route that’s right for you, or combine both!

🔹 Patience is key: Now the market is established, there’s less room for gold-rush-style purchases. Domains are less likely to be ‘flipped’ for huge profits now than in the early days. Holding them for longer periods may be necessary. But while patience is important, it's also essential to follow the market and trends to not overkeep the domains until the trend has gone.

🔹 Don’t jump on every fad: Pick wisely, as not every fad is going to become lucrative.

🔹 Engage with the community: It’s not something taught in schools, but there’s a whole domainer community out there! Many are happy to share what they know.

🔹 Learn from others' mistakes: Don’t register domains that are trademark infringements or obvious typos of another website.

🔹 Know where to sell: Use a reputable, fair seller – just like Spaceship SellerHub😉

🙏Thank you God, family, and friends. 🙏

Big congrats to the buyer — this is a remarkable name to own!

The 9-month young .Now TLD is proving itself to be one of the most—if not the most—exciting gTLDs ever. 

Think of it this way: what TLD could have entered the market late 2024, with some much competition—so many well-established TLDs—and score:

1) a $37,500 sale in less than 2 months
2) a $79,499 sale in less than 9 months

Both organic inbound sales.

And for that, a TLD not tied to any hyped-up trend – a gTLD in the truest sense of the G, like .Com.

Only .Now. We don't see any other TLD that could've made it work.

But – we think no one really sees .Now's true potential yet. We'll share this: for about two months we've had an idea for .Now – a vision. And with it, a special promo post where we'll lay it out. It's probably dropping in September or October. Stay tuned.

The sale happened on @sedo via the Buy Now option. The buyer was referred by Porkbun but ultimately chose Spaceship as their registrar. It will be submitted to DN Journal and NameBio shortly.

Atom​.com wasn't part of this sale – but shoutout to @atomHQ for spotting .Now's potential early and backing it from the start.

As much as we love our account manager at GoDaddy​.com, and we wish every domainer had someone as caring as Mauli in their corner: GoDaddy and Afternic have been a big disappointment. We don't think they've ever had more requests to add a TLD than they've had for .Now – from all of us. Despite that, they weren't there to support us in the first—and often the most difficult—year.

To their credit, registrars like 101domain, Dynadot, Namecheap, Spaceship, and Porkbun stepped up.

Has to be said: the rapid success of .Now wouldn't be possible without the steady progress new gTLDs have made over the years. It's impressive: in June alone, we sold 15 gTLD domains. For June, that's an unprecedented result. People want creative, memorable premium names for their businesses – a necessity in today's fast-paced world.

.Now investors – don't miss our post tomorrow (or shortly after). We just picked up another .Now via BIN on Atom (seller should be notified soon). And yes – we'll be buying more.

Once again, big congrats to the buyer on acquiring Love.now .

I did a deep dive into our 290 LTO deals at @afternic and discovered some valuable insights concerning cancellations, early payoffs, and trends.

📉 Cancellation Rates

Our raw cancellation rate was 26.9%, but that understates risk because it counts active deals as non-cancellations.

A better number is the resolved cancellation rate: cancellations divided by completed LTOs.

Historically, among our LTOs that have reached an outcome, about 59% completed successfully and 41% were cancelled.

⏱️ Cancellation Timing

Cancellations are heavily front-loaded. Obviously the more payments they make the less likely they are to walk away at the next payment. But at what point are they really committed?

Of our 78 cancellations, 28 (36%) made only one payment, 40 out of 78 (51%) made at most two payments, and 63 out of 78 (81%) made at most six payments.

Once a deal avoids cancelling after only one payment, its resolved success rate rises to about 70%. Once a deal avoids the early churn window and gets to around six payments, the resolved success rate rises to around 86-88%.

📆 Cancellation and Term Length

Most of our LTOs (87%) were in the 12-23 month range, so I'm not sure how statistically significant this data is. But there was a pretty clear pattern that the longer the length of the LTO, the higher the raw cancellation rate was.

The raw cancellation for LTOs less than one year was 25%, for 12-23 months it was 25.3%, for 24-35 months it was 31.2%, and for 36+ months it was 53.8%.

You might think the longer the term, the more manageable the monthly payments are, and the more likely they'll be to stick around. But in this dataset, longer terms were clearly riskier. Personally, I’d be cautious offering terms longer than 24 months.

💳 Cancellation and Monthly Payment

Looking only at 12-month LTOs, the raw cancellation rate was essentially the same for sub-$200 monthly payments vs $200-299 payments vs $300-499 payments. But interestingly, once the monthly payments reached $500+ the raw cancellation rate dropped by more than 50%.

That's somewhat intuitive though, someone committing to a $500+ monthly payment is probably more serious and well-funded.

🤔 Confusing Cancellations

Three buyers cancelled with only one payment left, which seems pretty unbelievable.

In 8 cases, a cancelled LTO later sold again shortly afterward — 6 through LTO and 2 through BIN. The data doesn’t include buyer identity, but given normal domain sell-through rates and the short timing, these were very likely buyers coming back after missing a payment or regretting the cancellation.

⚡ Early Payoffs

17% of completed LTOs were paid off early. Nearly half of early payoffs happened close to the finish line, but of the early payers, 32% paid off after only 1–2 payments.

📈 LTOs By Year

2023: 13 (53 annualized)
2024: 106
2025: 114
2026: 57 (137 annualized)

We're seeing a steady trend upward as LTOs stack up.

🎁 Wrap Up

I hope this helps you get a better picture of what you might experience if you enable LTOs.

The interesting takeaways for me were how heavily front-loaded LTO churn is, how longer terms reduce your odds of success, how little the monthly payment amount affects the odds except at the high end, and how more than 10% of cancelled LTOs still ended up in a sale shortly after.

Well is the "current" naming trend exemplified by "Montage" (short empty vessel) or is it exemplified by "UseMontage" (i.e. prefixing with a verb)?

If you're suggesting it is the latter, that is a naming convention in avoiding the aftermarket, not something that will help domain investors. Which was kind of my point... studying the sales teaches you "Montage" is a solid brand, studying ProductHunt incorrectly teaches you that prefixing with "Use" is an investable asset.

If you have to know to drop the "Use" to take something away from the ProductHunt discovery, then you're just adding extra work to the learning process and leaving room for mistakes. I think that is true for most of the examples I gave, not just the dictionary one.

Anyway, nice chatting with you.

It's certainly our job as domain investors to study and understand naming trends and conventions, but ultimately you're looking for names that people would pay a premium for in the aftermarket.

I'd be willing to bet a majority of ProductHunt launches are vibe coded startups on hand registered domains, and for the most part if you had beat them to the name they would simply have chosen a different name.

It's certainly a strategy, maybe as inspiration for hand registrations that you price low.

The top five ProductHunt launches today:

LobeHub․com
SocLeads․com
ReactVision․xyz
Shadow․do
UseMontage․ai

I doubt a single one of those is an aftermarket buy.

And there's a whole world of companies out there which would never launch on ProductHunt.

I would also study RaisingFi, CrunchBase, OpenCorporates, GitHub, and more as part of forming an overall acquisition strategy.

But if you want to understand what sells retail, study retail sales (which you said to not do) 😅

Me repeating it doesn't prove anything, your behavior does though.

Your principles of not letting people interact with your X content if they've been on the podcast of a site that didn't properly cite you? Do you hear yourself?

My main defense for not adding citations, which I'll repeat for the umpteenth time, is that the percentage of sales records that are even citable are incredibly tiny, one in about 100,000. Even if it required no extra server resources to query the citations on every search, and even if I could magically press a button and have all the citations in the database, it would still be a pointless thing to add. Nobody cares about it except for you.

Remove the venue column, which is applicable to 100% of sales, and replace it with a citation column which is applicable to 0.0001% of sales? Again, do you hear yourself?

Talk shit all you want. Point out my NameBio work schedule from six years ago when I was still working for Nat full time. Grasp at whatever straws you want to deflect from your behavior.

Doesn't change the fact that you're putting page views on an unmonetized site and X retweets over the good of the industry, just to stick it to a few bloggers who still manage to have plenty to write about without you. How utterly pointless.

Let's not forget, this whole discussion started from you pointing out a sale, inviting others to do the work to find the domain, and then you acted like a prick when I tried to compare notes with you. Then when I had the nerve to say you were being salty you went into attack mode, even though you've never said a word to me about citations in the history of NameBio.

Anyway, I'll let you get back to complaining about parasites and yelling at clouds and such.

I didn't say you expecting a citation is ridiculous, I said equating us to people rushing to publish articles and write social media posts is ridiculous. Especially knowing I go as far out of my way as possible to not draw any attention away from you. And in response to a post where I was trying to help with research no less.

You may have told Grok to be fair in the prompt, but it also read your posts, which were very harsh and grossly exaggerated the situation. We do not do aggressive SEO to rank the details pages well, we don't even have a sitemap for them. Almost none of our traffic comes from Google, by design. So no, we are not trying to steal your thunder or your long-tail search traffic.

You proved my point by showing that your name doesn't appear on our site at all. Because we never once tried to compete with you for breaking the news, throwing you a tiny citation at the bottom of an article as a shitty consolation prize, like the others you're trying to lump me in with did.

Why don't you tell Grok that your site is not monetized because you've built multi-generational wealth for yourself, and you're mostly surfacing high-dollar sales to bolster the value of your own amazing domain portfolio, and to help the industry garner mainstream interest. That you're not a journalist doing hardcore research to feed your family, and that you continue to do the research unabated even though you don't share the results with anyone.

Then ask what it thinks about your four-year strike, refusing to help the industry or yourself, because you didn't get enough hearts and re-posts and fake internet points.

Grok summed up my position pretty well:

"Practicality wins here. NameBio's real value is scale, verification, searchability, comps, and historical context—not breaking news. Most data truly is theirs or party-reported. Forcing a source field everywhere would bloat the DB and UX for negligible benefit. They run a service that helps the industry (free basic access, report tools, memberships for deeper use). Social engagement shows they're not total leeches. Kirikos's discoveries are edge cases, not the core product."

I agree that a citation in these rare instances of third-party reports would be the ideal thing to do. And you certainly deserve huge amounts of credit.

But I'm not going to add an extra database query to the many, many millions of page views we do every year just to look up if there's a needed citation on the few dozen sales you've uncovered. And I'm not going to spend countless hours to go back and find them all. Just so a small handful of people per month can mostly not even read the citation, and you maybe get a couple clicks out of it. That Rocket page you mentioned had 7 views in the last 30 days.

I say this with tremendous admiration and respect, but you've lost the plot. The reason you hunt for monster sales hasn't changed, obviously, because you still do it. But you being willing to share them somehow become about how viral you can go instead of the altruism and genuine love of the game that it started with.

That you would prefer I remove them if I'm not willing to add citations, when we're not even trying to compete with you for attention, speaks volumes and should really make you reflect on your motivations.

99.999% of the data we publish is not "discovered" by other people. It is observed by us. In rare instances it is reported by one of the parties, who either don't care about credit or put their own site as the venue for attribution.

As much as I respect you and your immense contribution to the discovery of many of history's most important domain sales, I'm not adding a database column just to cite the third-party sales you (or in extremely rare cases someone else) found. It would only be populated for one in every 100,000 sales or less.

I haven't ever written a single article about anything you found, and never wrote a dedicated social media post about it.

I just quietly add it with the old date (which I often have to look up myself), so it can come up in search.

It's already buried in nearly 7 million results and not pulling any attention away from you. And then I at least like and/or comment on your post, or sometimes repost it (without comment) depending on the situation.

To lump me in with everyone who is racing to leech attention away from you is beyond ridiculous.

Yes, we try to prevent people from stealing the whole database. But how many times have you seen me complaining about someone posting data we collected without attribution? It's zero. Even when it is our own personal sales that we only ever reported on NameBio, and they couldn't possibly have gotten it anywhere else. And it happens daily, not a few times per year.

I understand your frustration, but you don't need to take it out on me. I spent a few hours digging into the sale you mentioned, at your invitation, and you spat in my face when I tried to compare notes with you. Feel better?

I don't think your takeaway is correct here. It isn't proof that your domains bring the sales, in fact multiple large portfolios confirm that distribution networks produce a majority of sales. Landers generally only account for about 35-40% of volume.

Here's a recent discussion on de-listing from marketplaces, which also links to another older post about the makeup of aftermarket sales in the comments:

 nitter.poast.org/NameBio/status/2038913… 

Assuming you still list at Afternic, it's only proof that Sedo MLS provides very little extra coverage above Afternic DLS, and most partners of both prioritize Afternic listings.

We list a majority of our ~75k portfolio at Sedo, while being fully listed and majority landed at Afternic, and Sedo produces about 1 sale per year for every 4-5k names listed. Abysmal, but still five-figures per year in extra revenue that we likely wouldn't have had otherwise.

It's definitely a burden to keep multiple marketplaces up to date, and depending on portfolio size and your average sale price, I could definitely see an argument for de-listing from marketplaces that are under-performing.

So you're likely making the right call and won't regret it. Statistically with 1,750 listings you should only get a Sedo sale once every other year at best.

But I wouldn't jump to the conclusion that most sales come from the domain itself, because I guarantee you that isn't true.

For example, look at the attached screenshot of a search on "agent". You can instantly see that it has a higher sales velocity at the end rather than at the start. But you can also quickly see that being at the start results in a 33% higher average sale price than at the end.

This information is extremely valuable for domain spinners, appraisers, and AI agents, to better understand keyword values in Retail sales.

ABM just dropped one of the most valuable pieces of knowledge that has ever been shared in the domain industry, and most people are going to miss it because it was a reply to a reply.

In August of last year I did a pretty lengthy post breaking down the realities of the aftermarket, trying to help people understand what percentage of sales come directly from "for sale" landing pages, what percentage come from distribution networks, and of the network sales which come from each major distribution partner.

The reason I did that was to show the math on what happens if you list at Afternic and use their landers, versus using other landers with discounted commissions. What I essentially proved was that even if the alt lander has a 0% commission, you still end up worse off due to Afternic's commission penalty for not using their landers.

I'll link to that post in the replies if you want to do a deep dive and really understand the full picture. But in short, around 60-65% of domain sales come from Afternic DLS and Sedo MLS (the distribution networks), and the remaining 35-40% come from the "for sale" landers directly. This is confirmed by multiple large portfolio holders.

There were still two important questions that I was unable to answer though:

The first is what would happen if you fully delisted from Afternic, so they couldn't sell your domains at the 25-30% punitive rate while using alt landers. The theory a lot of people shared was that the network buyers, not being able to find you on the network, would still find you by typing in the domain.

I wasn't buying it. Sure, it'll happen sometimes, but I was almost certain it would be an extreme minority, and the move would be a major net negative.

My theory was that a vast majority of network buyers were either shown your domain as an alternative to what they were actually searching, or when brainstorming a bunch of different domains. And they wouldn't have found it without the network, because they weren't typing domains into their browser's address bar to check availability. They were using a registrar.

But I couldn't prove it because I've never fully delisted from Afternic and Sedo to find out, and I didn't know anyone who has and then talked about it. Until now.

Thanks to ABM we now have that missing piece of the puzzle; he said sales dropped 50% by delisting. That means if his sales breakdown was 40% landers 60% network, only 17% of network buyers would buy directly if it wasn't on the network. Or if his breakdown was 35% landers and 65% network, only 23% would buy directly if it wasn't on the network.

Let that sink in. Between 77% and 83% of network buyers will NOT buy your domain directly from your discount-commission landers if you are not on the distribution networks. If you scroll up on ABM's reply below, you'll see it was a reply to a comment I made predicting this "50% drop" outcome pretty much on the nose.

The second looming question is what would happen if you raised your prices on Afternic and Sedo to offset the higher commissions and then used your own landers with low or no commissions offering the domain at a lower price. A lot of people think this is "free money" for network sales by baking in the commission.

But I know that it will, for the most part, hurt your sell-through rate quite a bit. I can't quantify it, but I suspect it would almost definitely more than offset the commission penalties you were hoping to recoup. It just seems logical, if you hurt your STR on 65% of your sales to get a slightly better commission on 35% of your sales, you're probably going to lose.

Except in the situation where most of your domains are priced below $2k; at that level you can raise prices without affecting the demand curve.

I selfishly hope ABM will test this next by relisting at Afternic and Sedo, but at higher prices than shown on his NamePros Landers; enough that he would net the same wherever it sells.

That would answer the last remaining question surrounding the economics of the domain aftermarket: is it even possible to offset a commission by raising prices?

My money is on "no". But once we know that, we'd be able to fully model out all possible outcomes and make perfectly informed decisions to maximize revenue based on all the various marketplace commission structures and "for sale" lander options.

Regardless, I hope ABM stops this delisting experiment for both his and Jamie's sake. It's already been running long enough to learn everything there is to learn from it.

It's painfully obvious that a 50% drop in sales to save 15-20% on commission isn't a winning move. Let's say he was doing $1 million in sales a year and netting $800k after commission. Now he would have about $500k in sales, netting maybe $480k after transaction costs. That means he probably spent around $320k to learn this lesson.

We all owe ABM an enormous debt of gratitude for generously sharing what he learned with everyone.

We have 6.5 million sales records totaling more than $3 billion. How much more revenue do you think we make when someone reports a $2,500 sale? It's fractions of a penny at the most, if you could actually attribute any incremental revenue to it at all, which would be a massive stretch.

Considering the time it takes to review and approve that report, or grab it ourselves from social media, we actually lose money for every manually reported sale. But we still do it anyway, because not everything is about the money.

Marketplaces and brokers report because it attracts more sellers and buyers, which means they do more deal flow. It makes sense for them to incentivize reporting, because it's cheap marketing. One sale report could inspire someone to list their whole portfolio, which could generate tens of thousands per year in commission.

Sedo makes you pay them to not report it. Atom incentivizes agreeing to report it. Most other marketplaces are behind the times and do nothing.

As for individual investors, there are 850k+ people who use the site for free every year doing many millions of searches. Some who have benefitted from the data want to give back, although 100% of our users consume more data than they provide by many, many orders of magnitude.

Some do it for the clout, some do it for the pride of making on the daily chart, etc. Even paid users report sales just to be nice.

We can't incentivize reporting though. Partially because it might encourage fake reports just to get the incentive. Partially because the value of a single sale, unless it is a headline sale of six or seven figures, is so small there's nothing we can justify offering other than a high five. And people who report headline sales aren't going to be moved by a token incentive because, well... they be ballin'.

Make sense?

🚨 FREE access to the com/net drop order 🚨

Many domainers don't know this, but .com and .net domains don't drop randomly starting at 2pm ET — Verisign releases them in a specific order.

Knowing the exact order changes everything for those of you catching with Registrar APIs.

Instead of spreading out API calls across all your target domains that haven't released yet, you can focus 100% of your resources on one domain at a time.

Depending on how many domains you're going after, this could mean a 5x, 10x, or even 50x speed boost.

The big players have had access to this data for years through Verisign's Internet Profile Service reports. Now you can have it too.

Will you be able to compete with DropCatch on high-value names? No, although it's theoretically possible that you'd get extremely lucky.

But you will be able to destroy anyone who isn't using the drop order or is trying to catch by hand.

1. API endpoint (no auth or registration required)

I can't overstate how important this piece of advice is. We all get lowball offers, but how you respond can make a huge difference.

One time I received a $250 opening offer for a .org that I had on a "make offer" lander. I had purchased it for four-figures and expected mid five-figures.

Instead of firing off a snarky response, I responded saying thanks for the offer but we're too far apart, and showed a dozen close comps of .orgs selling for five and even six figures.

He responded back saying he was the buyer for many of those comps I had shown him. He added that he knew the value, but hey, he had to start somewhere. We ended up closing at $30,000 after a little bit of back-and-forth.

The domain wasn't something he had to have, he just wanted it for his collection, and it still isn't developed to this day. So if I had responded like a jerk or just ignored him entirely I'm pretty sure he would have moved on and found something else.

We also saw this recently when @dnx shared one of Josh's negotiations:

 nitter.poast.org/dnx/status/19908664574… 

He received a $5,000 offer on a name he was expecting $100,000 for. Instead of being rude he responded professionally, and ended up closing a deal at $52,700. They probably weren't bluffing and were actually considering alternatives, so if he was a difficult person to deal with they might have walked.

Watch the video all the way to the end, because it also serves as a great reminder to follow up multiple times. I needed that, it appears that I'm too quick to close a lead when it seems obvious that it won't go anywhere.

I know you didn't mention anyone by name. But she's the only one on the planet who owns a statistically significant number of xyz, she's 99% of reported xyz sales, and she's the only one sharing substantially all of her xyz sales allowing you to calculate an expected STR.

So you can't have an educated conversation about the xyz retail market without studying her portfolio results. Nothing else is relevant.

Take three-letter .com for example. I spent most of my career working for someone who owns more than 10% of all of the possible combinations.

He told me the STR is around 0.33% when priced in the six and seven-figure range, which means you need 300 to make one sale per year, or if you own one you should expect to sit on it 300 years.

So I can't own a single one and then be confused about why I haven't made a sale after three years, and say it must be because I'm not in the short-domain cabal. Are there people making retail sales who own only a couple? Sure...

But that's irrelevant to determining expected outcomes. It's random dumb luck when you're not playing the numbers game. A lightning strike. Luck is not an investment strategy.

There are only 18 reported xyz sales in the six-figure range. I can count on my fingers how many people have reported them who are not named Swetha. I don't believe any of them only owned a single xyz domain. Only 1 of the sales was three syllables: Capital․xyz. Only one of them was primarily an adjective: Stable․xyz. Do you see how amazingly well those fit for crypto though?

The odds were extremely stacked against you owning a single three-syllable adjective that is a stretch to shoehorn it into a very niche Web3 use case, where your breakeven expected value requires a Top 10 sale.

I do agree that the renewal wasn't relevant to why you didn't achieve a retail sale of that single domain during that short time. You only had a 1/67 chance of it happening during the three-year window. You would have had almost twice as good odds putting $7,500 on a single number in roulette... let that sink in.

But the renewal should have been extremely relevant to your decision to acquire it in the first place, both because it'll prevent you from holding it long enough to see a sale, and it'll prevent you from liquidating it.

Dropping the price doesn't materially increase your odds of a retail sale on a short time horizon, and wholesale you'd struggle to give it away when there's no time left on the registration.

Swetha's STR is low, the most sales she ever had in a year was 141 which works out to about 0.5%. That means if you own one xyz, the expected time to sell is about 200 years.

At her average selling price of around $20k, renewals would have to average less than $100 just for her to break even.

Yours was $540 per year, so statistically you should expect to pay $108,000 in renewals before it would sell, on top of the $6k acquisition price.

Even if you were hoping to sell it for $114k (almost six times Swetha's average) that would just be a break-even expected value.

This was essentially a very expensive lottery ticket with no burn-down value to the wholesale market due to the renewal.

I don't even think it's a good empty vessel for a brand, not many companies call themselves just "Luxury." It's too generic and more commonly an adjective than a noun, which begs people to react with "luxury what?" not "wow, nice brand". Look how the .com is used.

But the larger issue is that you didn't pick something which would work well for crypto and Web3, which are the types of companies that adopted the TLD. Luxury relates well to the physical world (cars, apartments, fashion, travel) not intangibles like crypto, NFTs, or other blockchain projects.

People need to understand that Swetha is playing a large numbers game with standard renewals, and as long as her average selling price is more than $3k she's guaranteed to win. Nobody else can play that game now because premium renewals will eat you alive. Negari cut out the middle man, which is all of us... let him.

Other investors who had random sales despite doing it on a small scale stacked the odds in their favor as much as they could. They had low acquisition cost and renewal prices, owned enough of them that they could reasonably expect a sale in their lifetime, took the time to understand the buyers and what they might demand, and then got very lucky on top of it.

That's my take on it anyway, as someone with no skin in this TLD.

Such an unclear way to do it, and support will tell you tough luck if the buyer already made the down payment.

text:
Domain story worth remembering: Back in April 2021, Google lost temporary control of google .com.ar.

The ccTLD expired without timely renewal, and an Argentinian user legally registered it for just ~$5. The domain was offline for roughly 3 hours before Google recovered ownership.

A critical reminder: Many country-code domains (.ar and more) do NOT support auto-renew or multi-year registration. Even big tech brands face huge risks without strict domain asset management.

I'm going to say "ICANN" and "policy", but don't immediately tune me out. I promise this is interesting.

Did you know that under ICANN's Transfer Policy for Inter-Registrar Transfer, the 60-day lock is listed under reasons a Registrar of Record "may" deny a transfer (Section 3.7), but it isn't in the list of reasons they "must" deny a transfer (Section 3.8).

 icann.org/en/contracted-part… 

What does this mean? The 60-day lock is a right of the losing registrar, not a responsibility. It's optional.

To illustrate this, the image below shows a before and after of the WHOIS as I transfer a domain that is eight days old between two of our registrars. We are also the registrant so no customers were put at risk.

It's unfortunate that choosing to enforce a 60-day create/transfer lock became the industry standard.

Especially in situations like aftermarket domain sales where a two-month wait might kill a deal. Even more so when you also own the marketplace that made the sale and you know the transfer request is legitimate.

Just saying...

Some claim Swetha's X suspension is evidence of fraud, but this doesn't add up. X isn't investigating domain sales — they lack the industry knowledge, connections, and access to do that. We have an API endpoint people can use to vibe code their own Top Sales widget:
 api.namebio.com/docs/#topsal… 

There's also an endpoint that gives access to our comps engine, which is useful for landers.
 api.namebio.com/docs/#comps 

That said, you have to implement caching to avoid getting rate limited or running out of credits too quickly, which can add some complexity. Nothing an AI can't figure out though.

We've experimented with hosted versions in the past. They barely send any traffic to us because lander visitors usually aren't interested in buying domains. And landers can generate tons of junk traffic so the hosting of it isn't trivial. Not really worth the trouble for us to provide as a drop-in service.

Maybe some day marketplaces and landing page providers like Afternic, Atom, Efty, DomainEasy, Spaceship, Sudos, etc. will offer it as an option you can enable 🤷‍♂️ With so much competition to replace DAN you'd think someone would innovate in that way, lol.

Hundreds of thousands of people per year benefit from the data, a small percentage like to give back as thanks. Even some people who don't regularly use the site share data just to help others or to further the industry. Some people do it for the street cred. Others do it to establish a public baseline for similar domains they own. Everyone has their own motivation.

We can't really incentivize sharing sales without the ability to 100% confirm them with the venues at large scale, which realistically is probably never going to happen. Many of them will cooperate to manually confirm large sales, but that's about it. Otherwise we'd just be inviting fake sales reports.

There's also the issue that a single sales record is worth fractions of a penny, unless it's a headline sale and then maybe it's worth tens of cents. If we offered an incentive strong enough that it would actually motivate people who can't find it within themselves, we would be bleeding money.

There are only a handful of people on the planet doing enough sales where if they shared 100% of them we could maybe justify comping them a membership. But they're obviously doing well enough that they wouldn't really care about this kind of motivation.

The only way I could maybe see it working is a lottery-style incentive, where sharing a sale gets you a number of entries to win something, but not a guaranteed benefit.

But again we could only go down this road if all the major marketplaces would allow us to confirm sales of any dollar amount at scale. For example, by having a button in their UI where a party can click and report the sale directly to us without having to bother with screenshots or filling out a form.

If you go to namebio.com/trends there's an explanation of Relative Strength. It's not a percentage of total searches, it's relative to the top search.

So for example if the top keyword had 5000 searches, and second place had 2500, they would be 100% and 50% respectively. That quickly tells you #2 is half as popular as #1 without us having to reveal the raw numbers.

If we did a percentage of total searches, they would all be very small percentages and it would be harder to quickly get the same sense of scale.

Take the @DNAcademy course, study sales reports on NameBio and @DNJournal , listen to as many @DomainSherpa podcasts as you can. Get educated.

Then pick up better domains that actually have potential buyers. Google, @dotdbcom , and OpenCorporates are good places to check for a pulse.

For buying, check the expired auctions, GoDaddy closeouts, subscribe to the @DomainSmoke newsletter. Probably don't hand-register any more names.

Once you have some sellable inventory, list them on @Afternic , @Sedo , @atomHQ , etc. with BIN prices and wait. You can also reach out to potential buyers to speed up the process.

What you have now is something that isn't a good fit for the extension but could be somewhat decent in .com, a misspelled tongue-twister that doesn't even mean anything, another one that makes very little sense and zero companies have that name, and UDRP bait. The odds of any selling are essentially zero.

Good luck!

The odds of success are very small though. I would wager 80%+ of domain investors have a negative ROI overall; half of which have probably never made a sale. And less than 0.1% have it figured out and make a great ROI with meaningful income.

Those groups also share a lot of overlap with people who don't subscribe to services. Thankfully there are thousands in between who do subscribe, even if your straw poll gives you a different perspective.

The odds of success would look wildly different if more people had the sense to invest tens of dollars in training and tools to help them more effectively deploy their thousands of dollars in capital. I'm not just talking about us, but also @DNAcademy , @dotdbcom , etc.

Instead they blow tons of money on garbage and most likely rage quit before making a single sale. Penny wise and pound foolish. I think it's a concerning sign of dysfunction in this industry more than something to make light of, especially now that you've made it to the other side of the fence.

Brokerage is the best ROI in the industry; little upfront investment and no carrying costs. Registrar is by far the worst; huge upfront costs and an absolute race to the bottom on margins.

The STR of expired domains is far from 100%, you're thinking purely of backorder auctions. Obviously the STR of preorders will always be 100%, that isn't a function of price though.

But if you look at registrars such as GoDaddy, Dynadot, Namecheap, etc. that auction expired inventory before it gets deleted, where no backorder is required, a very large percentage end without bids despite not having reserves.

Yes, STR is absolutely a function of price. But that curve is also shifted and shaped by quality. As you noted, a low enough quality domain will have a 0% STR at any price. Hence so many no-reserve expired auctions ending without bids.

At the other extreme, the quality of domains you own would have a 100% STR even in the five and sometimes six-figure range. In any case it looks more like a step-wise curve.

At the lower end of quality the steps might be at $2.5k, $5k, and $10k but the lowest step is 2% STR. One of your domains might be stepped at $100k, $500k, $1m, and $5m but the lowest step is 100% STR.

Most people are operating much closer to the low end than the high end. In that neighborhood, the curve is shaped and shifted in such a way that there is an absolute cap on STR below which dropping the price does not increase the buyer pool nor the chances of it selling, because you're still bound by demand (or lack thereof).

It makes very close to zero difference if you price an average quality domain at $1,250 or $2,500. This was confirmed by our own testing on tens of thousands of domains over several months, and Atom (Squadhelp at the time) independently observed the same phenomenon months later.

You can't engineer literally any STR on average quality domains simply by adjusting pricing. You would need to open up a new buyer pool by pricing into wholesale liquidation territory, or do outbound, to get it above the natural cap.

There's actually a reason you see 1-2% so often, it isn't a coincidence or domainer lore. It's the upper bound on an average quality portfolio doing passive retail sales with fair pricing in the first step or two of the spectrum.

Even if you send the price all the way into wholesale liquidation territory, it still has an extremely low chance of selling unless you actively promote it. Otherwise you need a domain investor to randomly think of it out of a pool of millions of possible domains, like it more than the thousands of auctions they have to choose from every single day, and pull the trigger within 12 months, which is very unlikely.

At this quality level it's almost entirely a function of time and RNG for which ones hit. As long as the price is in the same ballpark/step, what actually sold would have sold regardless, and it's just a choice of if you'd rather make $1,250 or $2,500 on the sale. Pretty easy decision.

Auction houses and registrars would warehouse the names for retail sale if they could get away with it. Remember Standard Tactics? For some reason the optics on this are worse than them liquidating the names and giving the previous owner nothing, even though it is the same thing.

Same reason most new gTLD registries went for premiums with retail pricing instead of wholesale liquidation. Cut out the domainer middle man.

It depends largely on where your current pricing is at. If you already have a majority of names priced around $2,500 or less, cutting your prices in half will have almost zero impact on the number of sales. You'll just make half as much money for what would have sold anyway.

I can 100% guarantee you it won't double your sales. Even if it did, that wouldn't be your break-even point because you'd need to replace twice as much inventory. Actually, if you're pricing most of your names around $1,500 you should raise your prices 50% not slash them, and use the extra money to scale up your portfolio to achieve more sales.

For consistently selling 20+ domains per month retail, I would rank the factors in this order:

1. Quantity
2. Pricing
3. Outbound
4. Quality
5. Luck

STR is like a bell curve when compared to quality, it's not linear. Garbage names will have a very low STR, but so will very high quality names. The STR on LLL․coms is around 0.3% which is pretty abysmal, at my old job the company owned about 10% of them. But when one hits you might be making six figures profit, possibly even seven.

If you already have average quality names that are reasonably priced, improving quality even more is not your path to doubling your number of sales, you'd either need to double the size of your portfolio or do outbound sales as a full-time job. Quality is your path to doubling your average selling price though, which is an equally good goal to have, maybe even better given VeriSign price increases.

To hit 20 retail sales per month you need a large portfolio of names priced in the sweet spot if you want to do it passively, or with a smaller portfolio you'd need aggressive outbound sales. For passive we're talking 15,000+ average names, or 30,000+ decent names, or 60,000+ crap names. That last one wouldn't cover renewals though.

I think more people in this industry need to get comfortable with outbound sales and putting in long hours. Buy a handful of names after researching who you could outbound them to, and don't buy any more until you've reached out to everyone multiple times. Rinse and repeat until you find what sells, and then start scaling.

Too many rely on #5 above. They don't have the quantity or quality to see a sale within a few years, and are too lazy to outbound, so even with fair pricing they're missing too many factors and don't have a shot.

Seeing clowns being clowns? Yup, unfortunately. I wasn't going to give it more oxygen, but since you asked... I've already acknowledged that screenshots can easily be faked; that's not news.

That's why I logged into Swetha's Afternic account, so I could see for myself without having to rely on screenshots. But generally we have to operate on some level of trust and mutual respect, which apparently some people are not deserving of.

I'm not sure why anyone would feel the need to "test" to see if they can submit a fake sale and get it approved. A child could do it. And apparently a few children have done it for no good reason, to the detriment of everyone.

I have to say though, I'm surprised that someone who makes it their business to spread the word about domain sales on Twitter would damage their own reputation by submitting fake sales, and then openly brag about having no integrity like it is some kind of "gotcha" moment.

Screenshots are a step above just taking someone's word about a sale and publishing it, but not much of a step. It isn't feasible to log in to everyone's marketplace/escrow/bank accounts to actually verify sales.

Escrow is currently the only place that will verify a screenshot if I pass it along to them, which I do on occasion. I wish more services would at least cooperate, or better yet report the sales in the first place, but this industry is far too broken for that to ever happen.

And apparently for some people that still wouldn't be good enough anyway. They'll just say the transaction actually happened but it wasn't arms length and was the registry or individual self-dealing. Which I'll give them is possible, albeit unlikely.

Short of being a government agency, it's impossible to 100% verify a sale and know it wasn't an inside job. Same goes for Web3, even with the blockchain showing the sales they could still be self-dealing.

So where does that leave us? We can either all be adults and try to foster a mature industry where we share legitimate data and try to grow the market for everyone. Or we can be a bunch of clowns and try to poison the data for the LOLs, and I'll just stop accepting private sale report all together.

You all can decide, but it's looking like it might have to be the latter.

.BOT domain SOLD via $23,399 LTO @afternic 

In this post we'll talk a bit about the sale—but mostly about the .BOT TLD in general, and why we predict it will be one of the most established gTLDs in the near future.

.BOT, a TLD from the Amazon Registry, began its existence in a different era. Calling it a non-AI or non-robotics era might be a stretch, but you get the point—December 2017 was a very different time.

Back then, .BOT was a restricted TLD, unavailable through standard domain registrars – making it a niche extension that domain investors couldn't even consider.

When ChatGPT came along, Amazon realized the times had changed and, in early 2023, ended the restricted period to prepare for the general launch of .BOT.

On October 30, 2023, .BOT was officially reborn as a standard ICANN gTLD – available to anyone through standard domain registrars, with no limitations.

Still, the launch wasn't heavily promoted by Amazon, and so what really happened is that the natural—hype-free—life cycle of .BOT has begun.

Here's why we predict it will become one of the major gTLD players in the near future. Let's start with the basic characteristics of a TLD:
● It's a 3-letter TLD, which is optimal – a standard set decades ago by .com, .net, and .org, which is visually the most pleasing, feels most secure, and is generally the easiest to pronounce.
● It's super easy to say and sounds modern and sleek – in this regard, it belongs alongside top-tier TLDs with clear, easy pronunciation—like .com, .app, .now, .bet, or .dev.
● It looks distinctive—creating unique names—and adds a futuristic touch.
● It is backed by a solid registry within the ICANN program.

Here are some potential use cases for .BOT:
● AI-driven projects and web apps.
● AI companion—ranging from on-chain and finance to romance.
● Automation, which will define our era.
● AI Agents – with actual use cases already in action.

And here's a very interesting one:
● Robotics. Elon Musk predicts that by 2040, there will be more humanoid robots than humans. And that's just humanoid – imagine the total number when you include all types of robots. We're about to be living in a robot world. So, what's the perfect TLD for robotics? Of course, it's .BOT. The hypothetical .ROBOT, though it would still be a strong one, has two syllables and it's a bit too heavy to be an ideal TLD.

Given its optimal TLD structure and futuristic potential, .BOT is, in our book, destined to succeed on a larger scale. The only question is when.

What about downsides? One potential issue is that the word "bot" still carries some negative connotations. We've all heard terms like "bot attack", which likely originated in the 1990s with the rise of Internet Relay Chat (IRC), where automated scripts—early bots—were used for both benign and malicious purposes. While the idea of 'bad bots' still exists, public perception of the word "bot" has been steadily shifting in a more positive direction. A major turning point was the emergence of ChatGPT, a chatbot that helped people associate bots with advanced, helpful AI.

Looking ahead, it's certain that "bot" will increasingly be used to describe physical robots as well, further embedding a positive, futuristic feel into the term's public image.

At this stage, we recommend going with a premium and/or uplifting name for your .BOT domain.

Now, let's talk about the .BOT $23,399 LTO sale:

What we can say is that it's a non-premium (non-dictionary) creative name, 5 to 10 characters long. The website is intended for a Web3/DeFi AI assistant / on-chain AI agent.

We'd love to reveal the name, however, since the sale is ongoing and a website is already live on the domain, we don't want the buyer being approached with non-elegant (any, in this case) offers. When investors share ongoing sales, there's an unspoken etiquette that others shouldn't contact the buyer, but whether that would be respected, we can't be sure.

The sale took place on GoDaddy. We've asked Afternic to confirm it by replying to this post.

Lastly, do we recommend investing in .BOT? If you find a good-to great-name with standard renewal, certainly. If you're planning to invest in a few dozen or more .BOT domains, we recommend being prepared to be at a loss for one to three years. Right now, not many people even know that .BOT exists. That will change. The TLD is already available at all major domain registrars (now including GoDaddy), and we hope Amazon will begin running promotions for .BOT in the coming years. The fact that entrepreneurs are already showing interest in five-figure purchases for non-premium names is a strong signal of where things are headed.

Giving any recommendations, we assume you understand what makes a good .BOT domain. For that, we'll end this post with a few .BOT use cases:

● Co.bot : Collaborative Robotics, Cobot, is a company focused on developing innovative robots designed to interact seamlessly with humans, emphasizing real-world applicability, predictable behaviors, and advanced hardware. Recently raised $100M per @Dommunity .
● Odd.bot : Odd​.bot is a Dutch agri-tech company developing autonomous mechanical weeding robots, like the Maverick, to eliminate weeds in high-value crops without chemicals, promoting sustainable farming. Recently raised 7-figures.
● Enso.bot : Enso is a marketplace offering AI agents built by experts to automate tasks, enhance efficiency, and drive growth for small businesses, providing affordable and scalable solutions. Recently raised 7-figures.
● Farm.bot : FarmBot is an open-source CNC farming project offering hardware kits and software for automated precision agriculture, enabling users to grow food at home, in educational settings, or commercially with a web-based control system.
● Streamer.bot : Streamer​.bot is a free, lightweight tool for Twitch and YouTube streamers that enhances live streams with customizable chat commands, automated alerts, rewards systems, and integrations like OBS Studio, allowing for interactive and dynamic streaming experiences.
● Resist.bot : Resistbot is a chatbot service that allows U.S. users to easily compose and send letters to elected officials, create campaigns, check voter registration, and find polling places, delivering over 40 million letters since 2017.
● Circular.bot : Circular is a platform providing advanced statistics and tools for arbitrage on the Solana blockchain, offering insights into wallet performance, trading volume, and transaction data.
● Me.bot : Me​.bot is an AI-powered personal companion app that organizes notes, chats, and diaries, integrating with your life to manage schedules, spark creativity, and preserve memories while prioritizing data privacy and security.

MyVehicle .com Sold for $105,000 via @Escrow_com 

Every journey has milestones that leave a lasting impression on our hearts. For me, MyVehicle .com will always hold a special place in my entrepreneurial story — not just for its value, but for the journey, faith, and patience it demanded.

I’m happy to share that MyVehicle .com has officially been sold for $105,000 via @Escrow_com , concluding a 60-month lease-to-own deal that began with a heartfelt negotiation and just wrapped up successfully. The negotiation took about 6 months, but the full payout and relationship spanned over 5 years.

We always remember our first range-breaker — that defining deal which resets what we once thought was possible. The automotive sector has played a huge role in my life. In fact, ElectricCar .com, which I sold for $180,000, was my first single-payment six-figure deal. But MyVehicle .com holds the title for my first agreed six-figure deal, structured over a long-term plan — and now completed in full.

The Backstory

I acquired MyVehicle .com back in 2018 via a NameJet auction. Around that time, I already owned ElectricCar .com, and my vision was clear: collect premium automotive assets that could define the future, especially as EV (Electric Vehicle) interest was just starting to surge.

MyVehicle .com stood out to me as a powerful umbrella term — versatile and broad, applicable across multiple facets of the auto industry. Over the years, I consistently received serious inquiries. In 2019, one interested party started with a $5,000 offer, which through discussion reached $25,000 — a fantastic ROI considering I had only held it for under a year. But I politely declined while keeping the door open, as I had long-term conviction that the name would eventually break the six-figure mark, even if some found that laughable back then.

The Deal That Tested Patience and Character

In February 2020, just as COVID fears were beginning to spread, our daughter came down with a flu. My wife and I soon followed with similar symptoms. Doctors told us to rest — back then, no COVID testing was available, and we had no way of knowing what it really was.

Amidst that, I received an unexpected email — the same person who had offered $25,000 six months prior was back. I immediately recognized his name and revisited our past conversation. We got on a phone call, speaking for over an hour. I walked him through facts, market trends, and data — highlighting that even at the time, the highest known public sale with the keyword “Vehicle” was VehicleHistoryReport .com for $31,000.

The buyer appreciated the insight, but had budget constraints. I remembered wise advice once shared by @BradenPollock : "Always try your best to help your customer find a solution." So, instead of walking away, I offered a structured plan.

Initially, I asked for $15,000–$20,000 as down payment, with the balance in monthly installments. Since the buyer preferred using a credit card for his initial payments, I knew I couldn’t expect more than $5,000 per month due to processing limitations.

So, we worked out a custom plan:

Down Payment Schedule (First 4 Months)

Month 1: $4,735 ($2,300 + $2,434.50 escrow fees)

Month 2: $4,750

Month 3: $4,750

Month 4: $4,750

Installment Structure

Months 5–15: $1,580 per month

Months 16–27: $1,000 per month(adjusted due to COVID-related constraints)

Months 28–60: $1,790 per month

A Lesson in Patience and Faith

As the deal unfolded, there were numerous delays and inconsistencies in payments — some of which are clearly visible in our transaction screenshots. The buyer often reached out asking for understanding due to market uncertainty.

Many times, I could have enforced my rights. Per Escrow rules, I could have emailed them, and if no payment was made in 7 days, I could have reclaimed the asset and kept all payments made up to that point. But I chose not to.

Why?

Because I believe in God, ethics, morality, and trust — even when tested. God gave me several such tests during this period. I saw each moment as a choice to stand by my values rather than chase short-term gain. I believe in positive vibe deal. Hence I always supported all of his requests.

And I’m glad I did.

With God’s blessings, the buyer fully paid off the domain last month, marking the completion of my first-ever agreed six-figure lease-to-own deal.

A Bittersweet Twist

Just 5 months after this deal began, Vehicle .com hit the market. I had recently completed my ElectricCar .com sale and had fresh capital to reinvest. Naturally, I wanted to grab Vehicle .com to round off my portfolio. I offered $75,000, but it eventually sold to another investor for $120,000. I was genuinely happy for the buyer. I believe in celebrating others after they’ve executed.

Reflecting on the Journey

Today, six-figure deals are a regular part of my business, with God’s grace. I’m now averaging six figures in domain sales monthly, with a consistent five-figure income stream from active lease-to-own agreements.

Beyond domains, I’ve been receiving great returns in other investments as well — from real estate, crypto, stocks, mutual funds, gold, and bonds — all showing exceptional CAGR.

Each of these has a story, and I may share more from those experiences another time.

Final Thoughts

Warren Buffett once said, “Don’t put all your eggs in one basket,” while @elonmusk Elon Musk countered, “You can put all your eggs in one basket — just watch that basket closely.” I admire both, and I try to find a balanced path across various sectors.

Life will always bring challenges. What matters is how we respond — how we show up for the tests life throws at us. Those are the exams we must pass to graduate to the next level.

This was more than a domain sale. It was a story of patience, conviction, ethical conduct, and divine timing.

Thank you again to God, my family, and all friends who’ve supported me on this path.

🙏🙏🙏

🙏 Grateful to God, Family, and Friends 🙏

MyForce .com Sold for $90,000 via @Escrow_com 

Not every deal is just about money. Some are about trust, intuition, and the quiet confidence that comes from walking the long road with the right values.

I’m happy to share that MyForce .com has officially been sold for $90,000 via @Escrow_com , structured as a 60-month lease-to-own agreement with the same incredible buyer who earlier acquired MyVehicle .com for $105,000.

What makes this story special isn’t just the amount — it’s the timing, trust, and energy behind the deal.

The Backstory

Incredibly, I acquired MyForce .com just 3 months before we agreed on the deal — through a @godaddyauctions . Yes, only 90 days of holding. But while the timeline was short, the decision wasn’t random.

At the time, MyVehicle .com was already in escrow. That deal had taken nearly 6 months of negotiation and structure. Through that process, I got to know the buyer — not just as a customer, but as a person. I understood his mindset, his mission, and most importantly — his integrity.

So when he expressed interest in MyForce .com, the dialogue was natural. He made a humble request: could I consider $90,000 over 60 months, with no down payment, and some flexibility?

I didn’t hesitate.

Why?

Because I already had something more valuable than a deposit: trust.

Deal Structure

Total sale price: $90,000

Term: 60-month lease-to-own via @Escrow_com 

Down payment: None (by buyer’s request, accepted based on strong past record)

Monthly installments: Starting at $1,000, increasing over time

Delays: Yes — multiple months saw late payments

Outcome: Every payment was made. Every challenge was met with communication. Every commitment was fulfilled.

Why I Acquired MyForce .com

The reasoning was simple:

=> I love the “My” prefix — personal, memorable, brandable

=> MyVehicle .com had already validated the “My+Keyword” strategy

=> And no — I wasn’t holding out hope that @salesforce would come knocking someday. LOL

But MyForce .com had presence. It felt strong. It felt like a brand waiting to happen — across fitness, energy, empowerment, even AI or defense.

And that feeling was enough.

A Lesson in Trust and Character

This deal taught me (again) that structure means nothing without spirit.

At any point, I could’ve enforced the contract, reclaimed the domain, and kept the payments. But that’s not who I am. That’s not how I do business.

I stood by the buyer — not because I had to, but because I wanted to.

And once again, doing the right thing led to the right result.

The Bigger Picture

I’ve come to realize that the fruits we enjoy today often come from seeds we planted years ago — even if we didn’t realize it at the time.

=> My crypto investments, built through a disciplined and patient approach, have delivered handsomely over the past few years.

=> I've been accumulating gold since 2009, never imagining it would quietly outperform the S&P 500 over a 20-year span — but it did.

=> Real estate, mutual funds, and equities have rewarded long-term conviction with 20–25%+ CAGR over 10+ year periods.

These aren’t “lucky wins.” They’re rooted in a belief system.

My philosophy is grounded in two simple ideas:

🌱 The Farmer

You plant. You water. You protect the soil. Some seasons are quiet. Others bring storms. But you stay consistent. And when the time is right, the tree bears fruit — not just once, but again and again.

🎋 The Bamboo

For years, nothing seems to happen. Underground, roots grow deeper. Stronger. Then, suddenly, in a matter of months — it rises 20 feet. Not because it grew fast, but because it was ready.

I treat domains the same way.

Sometimes the reward comes in 3 months — like MyForce .com.

Other times, it takes 3 years.

But the principle is always the same: faith, consistency, and patience.

Final Thoughts

MyForce .com was one of the shortest holds of my portfolio — but the lessons, trust, and impact will last far longer.

What began as a quick auction pickup became a $90,000 deal built on nothing but mutual respect.

With God’s blessings, my business continues to evolve — from six-figure monthly domain sales to steady lease-to-own five-figure income, and a growing, diversified investment portfolio.

But no matter how high we rise, I believe the roots — humility, trust, ethics, and faith — must run even deeper.

Thank you again to God, family, and all the friends who continue to support this journey.

.APP continues to gain momentum and is currently the most popular new gTLD – both in end-user registrations and aftermarket interest – with a significant lead.

.APP also regularly scores second place among all existing TLDs – behind only .COM – for projects launched daily on ProductHunt​.com, according to data from @LeanneMac . This is a remarkable result.

Why is .APP that successful?
● The basics: it's a 3-letter TLD, which is optimal – visually the most pleasing and secure.
● Strong, single-syllable pronunciation.
● We rank it as the most appealing TLD, and the second most aesthetic (after .BOT).
● Brand quality: .APP elevates brand names in its unique way, making them positive and iconic. A great example is Viral​.app, recently acquired for $100,000 by @mikey_starts . No other TLD could strengthen the brand as well as .APP does. The names we just sold — Alien and Purpose — are other great examples.
● It's backed by a solid registry (Google Registry) under the ICANN program.

And here's one of .APP's key strengths:

It's not a hype-based TLD. .APP entered the market in 2018, and since then it has been steadily building its position year by year, becoming stronger over time. This means that:

● It is not tied to a specific timeframe, but recognized simply as a new TLD — and therefore carries no risk of becoming "old" in the public's perception, as some once-popular TLDs already have.
● It is a well-established TLD that is set to thrive long into the future.

.APP hits a milestone: numeric domains now valuable in China.

Not many people know this, and this is a sign of the highest popularity of a primarily English-language TLD: this year, .APP reached a level where its numeric domains (such as 118​.app) have real value – which means .APP became popular in China, a fantastic market for domains.

With over a million registrations, tens to hundreds of thousands of brands and projects have chosen .APP for their domain. Here are a few prominent ones:
● defi​.app: A modular DeFi super app for wallet management, cross-chain swaps, yield, and trading.
● Linear​.app: A project management platform for software teams with AI-assisted product development tools.
● Shop​.app: Shopify's global brand for shopping, package tracking, and secure payment experiences.
● Foundation​.app: An Ethereum-based marketplace where artists and collectors buy, sell, and showcase NFTs.
● Owner​.app: A real estate management platform for property owners, landlords, and tenants.
● bsky​.app: A decentralized social networking platform built on the open AT Protocol.
● Betr​.app: A gaming super app offering real-money sports betting and casual arcade-style games.
● Viral​.app: A content management platform for creators with AI-powered campaign and performance insights.
● Gamma​.app: An AI-powered platform to instantly design, refine, and share presentations and documents.
● Cash​.app: A digital wallet platform with 57 million users and $283 billion in yearly payments.
● Mirage​.app: a frontier AI video creation platform – just rebranded from Captions​.ai, as spotted by @dommunity .

From Web3 and crypto brands to payment solutions, AI-powered platforms, real estate management, social media, gaming, and entertainment – .APP is being used widely across industries.

Our prediction: .APP will continue to be the most popular new gTLD for years to come. It has reached its current level through steady, consistent progress – and it continues to grow. Our top .APP sales are from the recent months.

Given the rising value of .APP domains, we also expect to see more six-figure .APP sales going forward – with the best .APP on TD, Go​.app, which we consider the strongest .APP overall, now priced at $1.5M.

I tested a bucket of 6800 very similar domains; 3396 landed on Afternic, 2410 landed on Spaceship, and 994 landed on Atom Premium. All listed on both Afternic and Spaceship with identical prices.

Listing on Spaceship has been excellent though. Based on historical data from their performance in Afternic DLS, I was expecting them to produce 2-3 sales per month for us without using their landers.

🧠 Step 1 — Why I Acquired HealthStrategy .com for $3,000

In April 2024, I acquired HealthStrategy .com for $3,000. It wasn’t just a keyword play or a data-driven flip. It was a deliberate decision backed by clear reasoning, long-term vision, and flexible thinking.

When I came across the name, it immediately stuck with me.

Most people associate the word strategy with investing, marketing, or business consulting — but rarely apply that level of thinking to health, even though it's one of the most important areas of life and enterprise. That disconnect intrigued me.

I felt that HealthStrategy .com filled a critical gap. It wasn’t a gimmick or trendy mashup — it was:

==> Straightforward

==> Authoritative

==> Positioned for enterprise-level or institutional use

It had all the ingredients of a brand that could anchor a serious platform — whether for a corporate wellness consultancy, a strategic AI-driven health startup, a health planning app, or even a government or NGO initiative focused on public health policy.

📊 TLD Metrics vs Brand Potential

When evaluating domains, I often check how many other TLDs are registered using tools like DotDB.com . It’s a useful signal — and I believe in checking all key metrics.

In this case:

HealthStrategy .com had only 15 TLDs registered

By contrast, a domain I sold earlier — iSoft .com — had 152 TLDs registered

Yet the final outcomes flipped:

iSoft .com → Acquired for $9,000 → Sold for $60,000

HealthStrategy .com → Acquired for $3,000 → Sold for $100,000

This highlights an important truth in domain investing:

✅ TLD count is helpful, but not everything
✅ Every asset class is unique
✅ Brand clarity, context, and timing often matter more

🎯 Brand-First Decision Framework

Before I make a purchase, I always evaluate:

==> How the name sounds as a brand

==> Whether it makes semantic sense as a pair

==> How trustworthy or credible it feels in its industry

==> The strength of comparable sales in the niche

Only after those boxes are checked do I let gut instinct weigh in — and even then, it plays a supporting role, not a leading one.

In this case, I wasn’t influenced by how many TLDs were taken. I focused on the message the name delivers and how easily a serious company could build authority, trust, and inbound business using it.

Most of my best-performing sales in the high five to low six-figure range haven’t followed rigid, traditional investment playbooks. They’ve come from balanced judgment, thorough research, non-obvious positioning, and a willingness to wait.

That’s exactly what this was.

I dug into our Atom offers going all the way back to 2021. There were 110 to review and 48 were successfully closed, so clearly they're capable of closing from the offer center.

That said, I think there's definite room for improvement regarding qualifying leads before putting them into the offer center, and following up with the parties.

Of the 62 that didn't result in a sale, this is a breakdown of the reasons:

15% - Just too far apart on price, either we declined or buyer declined. Out of their hands.

8% - We missed the offer email and the broker never sent a follow-up. Usually they're good about this.

31% - We accepted the offer, either outright or after some back and forth, but the buyer didn't pay. This speaks to poor lead qualification.

47% - The buyer ghosted during negotiation. An overwhelming majority of these were us telling Atom to use the initial offer as the floor, meaning to try for more but ultimately just get a deal done. Most of the ones they did close were probably a similar situation though.

It would also be nice if they put some effort into updating the status in the offer center. Of the 48 that sold, one was marked Closed / Domain Purchased, one was marked Accepted, and all the others still have a status of Negotiation.

text: I understand your point, you're missing my point. Studying what people hand register when they try to avoid the aftermarket, and then intuiting what they would have named themselves if they were real companies, and then using that to back your way into an understanding of naming conventions is a really roundabout way to do it. You were only able to draw actual, valuable conclusions from it because you already have industry experience. People who don't already know what they're doing will make a lot of mistakes studying ProductHunt, because they won't understand how to modify the name to make it not be hot garbage. It's much more direct to just study what people paid a premium for. And your "discoveries" on what is trending NOW has basically been Branding 101 since the early 2000s, ever since companies abandoned EMDs like Pets․com and Diapers․com. Short, one or two word empty vessels (i.e. abstract) that pass the radio test. Although Verb + Noun is generally a way to avoid the aftermarket. Look at retail sales $5,000+ for each year of the past 20 years and you'll see the same "hot naming trends". You don't need to see that UseMontage․ai is trending on ProductHunt now to back your way into the "up to the minute" knowledge that "Montage" would make a decent brand. You could have known that in 2011 when Montage․net sold on Sedo for $3,100 or in 2013 when they sold Montage․org for $4,988. Instead you're learning it more than a decade later 🙄
